pretreatments.description: Dilution with water (WP): Olive oil and OMWW residues were diluted with tap water to a concentration of approximately 10% w/w of TS (33 g OP to 77 g OMWW). This was considered a pretreatment process (Section 2.4) and was tested to increase biogas production, mitigating acidity and polyphenol content. It showed a significant increase in biogas yield (approx. 13.5 L/L) with a CH4 concentration of 74% v/v (Section 5.1), though it was not energetically sustainable due to low energy consumption (ESI=8.62).

Basic Pretreatment (BP): Mixture was treated with 2 N NaOH until pH 12 was reached and stirred for 24 h at 30°C to neutralized with 2 N HCl before inoculum. This was a chemical pretreatment intended to improve hydrolysis and create beneficial effects on lignocellulosic materials via saponification, increasing porosity (Section 3.1).

Salt Pretreatment (SP): Mixture was treated with metal salts at 5 g/L concentration (FeSO4, FeCl3, MnSO4, CaCO3). The process involved adding solid salts to achieve pH of 2, mixing for 30 min, and neutralizing with NaOH. This pretreatment was tested for its effect on biogas production and organic matter abatement (Sections 3.2, 5.3). Salt types (Fe2+, Fe3+, Mn, Ca) were considered in this category.

Ultrasonic Pretreatment (USP): Physical pretreatment using ultrasonic waves at 1.8 kW power for varying doses (8000 kJ/L or 750 kJ/L). The aim was to break down complex chemical structures (lignin, cellulose) to increase surface area for bacterial degradation (Section 3.3). High dose (8000 kJ/L) and low dose (750 kJ/L) tests were performed.

Combined Pretreatment (CP): Combination of Ultrasonic Pretreatment (USP) with Salt Pretreatment (SP) or CaCO3 (CP_Ca) and FeCl3 (CP_FeIII). Specifically, the ultrasound was applied first at high dose (8000 kJ/L) followed by salt addition (Section 3.4).
